stories.headline: Update: Pentagon Iran War Costs Top $47 Billion as UN Watchdog Questions Tehran's Uranium Stockpile
stories.summary:
U.S. military spending in the Iran war has surpassed $47 billion, exceeding the Pentagon's July estimate by more than 25 percent, according to internal Defense Department figures obtained by Reuters. Munitions replenishment accounts for the largest share, at more than $29 billion, alongside more than $6 billion in equipment replacements.

The estimates do not include the cost of repairing damage to U.S. facilities targeted by Iranian drone and missile barrages, according to the report. The figures give the first detailed picture of the financial toll of the conflict as it continues to shape American politics a week before the midterm elections.

Fox News live coverage reported that President Trump hailed the latest U.S. strikes on Iran, while the United Nations nuclear watchdog raised alarm over Tehran's unverified uranium stockpile. Inspectors have been unable to confirm the location and condition of the material, fueling concern about Iran's nuclear capabilities. Peace talks and the status of the Strait of Hormuz remain central to the coverage.

Supporters of the administration's approach argue the strikes are necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and to restore deterrence. Critics, including many Democrats, point to the mounting cost and the absence of a clear diplomatic endgame. Trump has recently said it is "decision time" on Iran, framing the choice as a deal or a decisive finish to the conflict.

stories.headline: Federal Prosecutors Move to Charge James Comey for Third Time, This Time Over Leaking Defense Information
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors have taken steps to charge former FBI Director James Comey with leaking national defense information, according to a three-page court filing. It is the third time the Justice Department has moved to bring criminal charges against Comey, a longtime critic of President Trump. The filing, a criminal information filed in Washington, D.C., contains two counts and few details.

Comey's lawyers said in separate court papers that the case stems from an alleged disclosure of classified information to the New York Times in October 2016, while he led the FBI. A criminal information is a charging document filed directly by a prosecutor, unlike an indictment, which requires grand jury approval. Comey's attorney Patrick Fitzgerald said two earlier teams of prosecutors investigated the alleged disclosure during the first Trump administration and both decided no charges should be brought. His team has filed a motion to dismiss.

In a Substack video on Monday, Comey called the charges an "appalling abuse" of the Justice Department and said, "I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people." Former federal prosecutor Glenn Kirschner told the BBC the case may exceed the 10-year statute of limitations and called it a "revenge-fuelled attempt" by Trump. Law professor Jessica Levinson noted that cases against other Trump adversaries have had varied outcomes.

Trump has repeatedly called for Comey's prosecution since firing him in his first term, after Comey opened the investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. Supporters of the prosecution argue that mishandling classified information should be pursued regardless of the defendant's profile. The court will now consider the motion to dismiss.

stories.headline: Trump Proposes Loosening Methane Rules for Oil and Gas Producers
stories.summary:
President Trump announced a proposed rule to ease methane emission requirements for oil and gas producers during a campaign rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night. He said the EPA plans to ease regulations aimed at curbing methane leaks. The announcement came during his second Texas stop of the day, intended to boost the Senate campaign of Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton a week before the midterm elections.

The administration presented the move as part of its effort to boost domestic production and lower fuel prices. Higher energy costs have weighed on Republican candidates this election cycle, and the proposal is aimed at the oil-heavy region where Trump was speaking. Industry groups have long argued that leak-detection and repair requirements are costly and burdensome.

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas and a major contributor to climate change, and environmental groups and many Democrats have opposed efforts to weaken limits on leaks from oil and gas operations. They argue that curbing methane is among the fastest and cheapest ways to slow warming. The proposal must go through the formal rulemaking process, including public comment, before any change takes effect.

stories.headline: CDC Deputy Director Jennifer Shuford to Leave After Less Than Five Months
stories.summary:
Dr. Jennifer Shuford, deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, will leave the agency on Nov. 12, a spokesperson said. Her departure comes less than five months into the job, which she started in June after Trump announced her appointment in April. In a statement, she said she was leaving to spend more time with her family and thanked Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Satish Pillai, who leads the agency's Ebola response, will serve as acting deputy director while the CDC searches for a permanent successor. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz, confirmed by the Senate in August, announced the news to staff in an email Tuesday, praising Shuford's leadership in an "exceptionally demanding" environment. Shuford previously served as Texas's chief state epidemiologist and health commissioner, and oversaw the response to last year's West Texas measles outbreak.

Her exit adds to leadership turnover at top health agencies under the Trump administration. Kennedy fired CDC Director Susan Monarez in August 2025, and the agency lacked a permanent director for about a year. Principal deputy director Ralph Abraham stepped down in February, and Allison Arwady left in June. Calley Means resigned last week as a senior HHS adviser, and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary resigned in May.

stories.headline: U.S. Military Says Strike on Alleged Drug Boat in Eastern Pacific Kills Five
stories.summary:
The U.S. military said it attacked a boat it accused of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Tuesday, killing five people. The strike brings the number of people killed in U.S. boat strikes to at least 240 across more than 70 attacks since the Trump administration began targeting what it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025.

As with most such announcements, U.S. Southern Command said the vessel was targeted along known smuggling routes and that "intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narcotrafficking." The military did not provide evidence that the boat was carrying drugs. A video posted on X showed a small boat in the water before it was engulfed by an explosion.

President Donald Trump has said the United States is in "armed conflict" with Latin American cartels and has defended the strikes as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs and fatal overdoses. Critics, including some Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars, question the legality and effectiveness of the strikes, noting that much of the fentanyl entering the U.S. comes overland from Mexico. The Pentagon's watchdog said in May it would examine whether the military followed its targeting framework, though not the legality of the strikes.

Tuesday's strike is among a few that followed Secretary of State Marco Rubio's September pledge to seek approval from regional allies. Rubio has said the U.S. can act unilaterally but prefers to work with partners, while adding that the military would "still blow up ships if need be."

stories.headline: Alexander Brothers Each Sentenced to 30 Years in Prison in Sex Trafficking Case
stories.summary:
A federal judge in New York sentenced Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, to 30 years in prison each for drugging and raping dozens of women over decades. Judge Valerie Caproni told the men, "Your conduct was monstrous," and said their crimes "wreaked havoc" on victims' lives. The brothers were found guilty in March.

The court heard from 12 victims on Tuesday, including one who did not testify at trial. Many urged the maximum sentence of life in prison. Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers "honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury" and were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them." Victims described lasting trauma, and one said Tal Alexander threatened her when she planned to come forward.

Defense attorneys sought 15-year sentences, arguing the men had become devoted fathers whose families would suffer. All three continued to profess innocence in court. Caproni rebuked them for refusing to acknowledge wrongdoing, asking, "How can someone who never acknowledged the wrongs they did be rehabilitated?"

She imposed 30 years for certain counts and 20 years for additional counts, to be served concurrently. At the five-week trial, 11 women testified that the brothers lured them with gifts and trips to places including Aspen and the Bahamas, where they were drugged and assaulted. Several said they were minors at the time.

stories.headline: DCCC Pushes Ads Targeting Republicans on AI and Data Centers in Key House Races
stories.summary:
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is pushing advertising that targets Republican candidates over their records on artificial intelligence and data centers in dozens of key House races. The effort, detailed in a report from the Tech Oversight Project shared first with The Hill, reflects the growing role of technology issues in the midterm elections one week before voting.

The push follows rising backlash over data center construction, which has become a campaign issue as communities raise concerns about energy costs, environmental effects and local land use. Democrats are seeking to tie Republicans to those frustrations.

Supporters of data center development argue the facilities bring economic benefits. Texas billionaire developer Ross Perot Jr. said at a Bloomberg Invest event in Dallas that data centers are good for communities and help the United States compete with China on AI.

The debate comes as the AI industry draws heavy investment and public attention, including Anthropic's planned public listing. How voters weigh technology costs against economic promises may factor into close House contests.

stories.headline: Update: Lula's Win in Brazil Dents Trump's Ambitions for Latin America, Analysts Say
stories.summary:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva declared in his victory speech that "Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," a message aimed at Washington. His defiance of what he called U.S. interference, including tariffs tied to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, helped fuel a patriotic campaign message.

Trump said, "I like Lula, we get along well," and "I didn't take sides," while also calling the election "terrible" and "rigged." He did not explicitly endorse Flavio Bolsonaro, who has refused to recognize the result. The two leaders met in the Oval Office last year after tariffs were reduced, though they have since risen again.

Latin America has moved right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru electing presidents aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has pursued U.S. dominance in the hemisphere under a strategy dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine." Chatham House's Christopher Sabatini said Trump saw Brazil as the "10th and biggest prize."

Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and a Bolsonaro victory would have strengthened that bloc. Lula's win now complicates Washington's regional plans.

stories.headline: Update: US Orders Non-Emergency Personnel to Leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi Strikes Escalate
stories.summary:
The State Department on Tuesday ordered non-emergency U.S. government personnel and their families to evacuate Saudi Arabia after a surge in missile and drone strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure across the kingdom. The security alert said Iranian-supported Houthi forces have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, causing civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.

The alert warned that the hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area." Flight operations remain badly disrupted, with only limited routes operating from Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and significant delays at Jeddah and Dammam. U.S. officials urged private citizens to use extreme caution and consider overland exits such as the King Fahd Causeway. They also reminded travelers of local rules barring the filming or sharing of attack sites and counter-missile activity.

The order follows earlier coverage of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Egypt's parliamentary backing for a defense offer to Riyadh. It comes amid heightened U.S.-Iran tensions, with President Trump having framed the moment as "decision time" on Iran. Fox News live coverage also reported Iranian officials discussing regional security and urging Middle Eastern states to reduce U.S. influence. The evacuation order is the clearest sign yet that Washington sees a risk of wider regional conflict.

stories.headline: Update: Flávio Bolsonaro Reportedly Flees Brazil After Election Loss and Passport Order
stories.summary:
Flávio Bolsonaro left Brazil within hours of losing the presidential runoff to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and being ordered to surrender his passports, the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported, citing allies of the conservative senator. Bloomberg reported he was on a plane to the United States after missing the deadline to hand over his passport.

Argentina's government denied that Bolsonaro had entered that country, according to the report's accompanying coverage. The reported departure follows his refusal to concede the race, which Lula won to secure a fourth term.

The development raises questions about legal proceedings facing Bolsonaro and the stability of Brazil's post-election period. Brazilian authorities have not yet detailed what action they will take over the missed deadline. Supporters of Bolsonaro have disputed the legitimacy of the process, while Lula's allies have called for the court orders to be respected.

stories.headline: Federal Agents Search Beverly Hills Home in Eric Swalwell Misconduct Investigation
stories.summary:
Federal law enforcement agents searched a Beverly Hills home early Tuesday as part of an investigation into Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress amid a wave of sexual misconduct allegations. A law enforcement official and two people familiar with the probe confirmed the search to the Associated Press.

The home belongs to wealthy developer Stephen Cloobeck, a Swalwell donor. The search ties the developer to the sexual misconduct inquiry, though details on what agents sought or why the property was targeted were limited.

The search marks a significant escalation from the allegations that forced Swalwell from office into an active federal criminal investigation. No charges have been announced. It is unclear whether Cloobeck is a subject of the inquiry or a witness, and further developments are expected as investigators review evidence.

stories.headline: Egyptian Editor Lina Attalah Detained After Court Orders Mada Masr Closed
stories.summary:
Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian outlet Mada Masr, was taken into custody after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers said. The New Cairo Misdemeanours Court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds, about $53,500, the maximum penalty, and she will be held until it is paid.

Amnesty International called the verdict "a crushing blow to press freedom." The Committee to Protect Journalists said Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is a vital source of critical reporting and that it repeatedly sought a license under a 2018 media law but was rejected or ignored. During the hearing the judge cleared the courtroom of nearly everyone but Attalah, her defense team and a rights group head, then denied defense requests and appointed his own lawyer for her.

The ruling comes weeks after six journalists at the fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the banned Muslim Brotherhood. Egypt holds 25 journalists in prison, according to CPJ, and rights groups say President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has overseen an unprecedented crackdown on dissent.

stories.headline: West Warns of Famine Risk in Sudan as Civil War Grinds On
stories.summary:
The United States and 30 other Western states issued a joint statement warning of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan. They urged the warring parties to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine. The statement was published by the State Department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website. Signatories include EU states, the United Kingdom, Canada, Switzerland and Norway.

The statement estimates that 19.5 million people, or 41 percent of Sudan's population, face high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million at emergency levels of hunger. It warns that the number of children suffering severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000 without immediate action. Signatories blamed conflict as the main driver of hunger, citing damage to infrastructure and disrupted food production. They also cited systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has reduced rainfall and deepened drought across more than half the country.

The war began in April 2023 as a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, and it has displaced 14 million people. The World Health Organization has described it as the world's worst humanitarian crisis. Yusuf Roble of Islamic Relief East Africa said people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted and that "there is very little to survive on." He said only 40 percent of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September. The statement says the warring parties bear primary responsibility for easing the suffering and calls on them to allow full, safe and unimpeded access for aid.

stories.headline: Colorado and Washington Voters to Decide on Banning Transgender Girls From Girls' School Sports
stories.summary:
Colorado and Washington, both reliably Democratic states, will put proposed bans on transgender women and girls in female sports competitions before voters next month. Activists went around legislators, who had rejected such bans, to place the measures on the ballot. It is the first time the issue has gone directly to voters. The Colorado measure also covers college sports. Arizona has a measure to extend an existing ban to private schools, and Nebraska has one to write an existing law into its constitution.

Supporters say the measures protect women and girls and preserve separate spaces, and they are optimistic of passage. They argue success could open the door to similar efforts in states where lawmakers have blocked bans. Twenty-seven states, including all where Republicans control both the legislature and governorship, already have such laws, and the Supreme Court has upheld state sports bans. President Donald Trump has taken steps to roll back transgender rights.

A June Quinnipiac University poll found about 7 in 10 registered voters think transgender women and girls should not play on female teams, while about a quarter disagree. Democrats are split roughly evenly. Some Democratic leaders nationwide are recalibrating their approach to the issue. Advocates for LGBTQ+ rights oppose the bans; Chris Melody Fields Figueredo of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, which supports LGBTQ+ rights, called 2026 "a testing ground for the future." A Colorado political scientist noted the lack of public polling makes the outcome there hard to predict.

stories.headline: Mbappé Apologizes for 'Ill-Judged' Mao Remark After Chinese Brands Drop Him
stories.summary:
Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé apologized for comments about Mao Zedong after Chinese brands cut ties with him. On the French talk show The Bridge, he said the meme that makes him laugh most was one with a video of "a Chinese dictator" with his face superimposed. The joke plays on his nickname "The Dictator." He said his comment was "ill-judged" and that he understood it hurt many people in China and Chinese communities worldwide.

Eastroc Beverage Group, China Mengniu Dairy and Dongpeng ended partnerships after their stocks reportedly fell, according to Bloomberg. Fox News reported that his Weibo and Xiaohongshu accounts were frozen and that state broadcaster CCTV stopped airing Real Madrid and other La Liga matches. Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people would be met with opposition from all sectors of society. La Liga also apologized.

Mao remains revered by the Communist Party, though his rule left millions dead; Fox News put the toll at tens of millions. The furor began Monday night when Chinese football forum Dongqiudi called the comments inappropriate. Some Chinese users have questioned the reaction, though supportive voices are rare on the tightly controlled internet. The episode shows how commercial exposure in China can hinge on sensitivity to political topics.

stories.headline: FTC Sues Dollar General Over Checkout Overcharging
stories.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission sued Dollar General on Monday, alleging the discount retailer repeatedly charged customers more at checkout than the prices advertised on shelves, in weekly flyers and on its website.

The complaint says the pricing problems persisted for years despite thousands of failed inspections, tens of thousands of consumer complaints and multiple enforcement actions. The case targets one of the largest discount chains in the country, whose customers are often lower-income households sensitive to small price differences.

The suit adds to regulatory scrutiny of retail pricing practices. Further details on the relief the FTC is seeking and any response from Dollar General were not available in the initial reporting.

stories.headline: Norway and Finland Leaders Hold Rare Joint Call With Putin on Ukraine Peace Efforts
stories.summary:
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a joint call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, the first contact between European leaders and the Russian president since French President Emmanuel Macron spoke with him in July 2025. The call was held from Helsinki. The two leaders said the aim was to discuss "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, and stressed that their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole."

Stubb described the call as "frank and substantive" and said the war's outcome would have a direct effect on European security. Støre said the war carries "enormous human and material costs." After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and NATO policies were prolonging the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Moscow routinely accuses European governments of prolonging the conflict by arming Ukraine, though Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last weekend that having a European negotiator at the table would be "good."

The call follows talks in Oslo on October 20 among the two Nordic leaders, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, after which Witkoff traveled to St Petersburg to meet Putin. Ukraine, Russia and the United States subsequently agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had halted for months. Zelensky, who spoke with the Nordic leaders afterward, said part of their conversation with Putin centered on the trilateral talks planned for Abu Dhabi in November.

Not all European governments welcomed the move. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" and noted the call "hasn't been co-ordinated with any of the rest of us." The contact comes as relations between Washington, Kyiv and European allies have strained since President Trump agreed to lift some sanctions on Russia, allowing it to export oil to the United States.

stories.headline: Appeals Court Declines to Block Counting of 20,000 California Mail Ballots
stories.summary:
A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block California from counting about 20,000 mail ballots that the Trump administration says were cast by noncitizens. In a 2-1 ruling, the court rejected a Justice Department demand that election officials segregate the ballots while the underlying dispute is litigated, days before the midterm elections.

The Justice Department contends that roughly 20,000 registered voters in California are not US citizens and that their ballots should be set aside. The administration's position is that ensuring only eligible citizens vote requires holding the ballots separate until the question is resolved. California officials have resisted the demand, and Governor Gavin Newsom accused President Trump of mounting an "assault on democracy."

The ruling is a procedural denial of emergency relief rather than a final decision on the merits, so the broader legal fight over the voters' eligibility continues. The outcome matters because of the timing: ballots are being counted as the midterms near, and control of Congress is at stake. Supporters of the administration frame the effort as basic election integrity, while Democrats and California officials characterize it as an attempt to disrupt lawful voting. Further litigation or an appeal to the Supreme Court is possible.

stories.headline: Update: Anthropic IPO Filing Leads $235 Billion Day of AI Dealmaking
stories.summary:
Anthropic filed paperwork on Monday for an initial public offering that could become the largest ever, potentially seeking to raise a record $100 billion. The filing capped a day of AI-related deals totaling about $235 billion, nearly 1% of US GDP, according to Axios. The company would be the first major pure-play AI firm to go public.

The prospectus, reported at 355 pages, includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. These include warnings that the company's own technology could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, as well as concerns about AI models engaging in blackmail. It also discloses roughly $650 billion to $750 billion in computing commitments, a scale of obligation without precedent for a newly listed company.

The same day, SpaceX secured $40 billion in debt financing to lease GPUs, the chips that power modern AI systems. Axios noted that Wall Street is financing the AI buildout in real time, making the sector central to the American economy at unusual speed. Investors reading the prospectus found both reasons for optimism, including very high revenue per employee, and warning signs tied to the size of the spending commitments. The listing is planned for the Nasdaq, and the pricing and timing of the offering will be closely watched as a gauge of investor appetite for AI.

stories.headline: Netherlands Pulls Out of 2027 Eurovision Over Israel's Participation
stories.summary:
The Netherlands will not take part in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest, public broadcaster NPO announced Tuesday, reversing a pledge made last month to return. NPO media director Jurre Bosman said Israel's participation "elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division." NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the broadcaster could not find a suitable format and concluded it is "too early" to participate.

The Netherlands was one of five countries, with Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia, that boycotted the 2026 contest over Israel's inclusion, amid criticism of Israel's military actions in Gaza and the wider Middle East. Ireland has also said it will skip 2027, and the head of Spain's public broadcaster has voiced support for a boycott. The Czech broadcaster has also withdrawn, citing spending cuts.

Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" but respected the decision, adding that Eurovision "matters in a divided world." Organizers have announced changes to address the divisions, including barring any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting and altering the voting system. The 2027 contest will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria, on May 15, following Dara's win in Vienna this year. The Dutch will still broadcast the event.

stories.headline: Update: Israel Votes in Pivotal General Election as Regional Tensions Mount
stories.summary:
Israelis went to the polls on Tuesday in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history. Security and democracy have emerged as central issues. Many analysts fear neither of the two leading political blocs will win enough seats for a majority, which could mean weeks or months of coalition negotiations.

The vote follows a tense week. Israel imposed movement restrictions on Palestinian workers in the West Bank after two Israeli soldiers were killed by two Palestinian gunmen on Friday. Disaffection has often depressed turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push in that community to remove the right-wing governing coalition. More than half a million young people were also eligible to vote for the first time. Disputes over drafting ultra-Orthodox men into the army have strained Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition.

The election comes as the region remains volatile. Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have escalated, and Israel recently held its largest military drills in years amid tensions with Iran. Separately, a Syrian health official said an attack on a village killed five people, including women and children, and a shooting in the village of Hmoud killed nine Christians; no group has claimed responsibility. The State Department has also adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts in the region.

Official results are expected in the coming days. Coalition talks are likely to determine who leads the next government, with Netanyahu seeking re-election.

stories.headline: Trump Rallies in Mississippi as Parties Make Closing Midterm Arguments
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump campaigned in Mississippi on Monday as part of a closing rally blitz, eight days before the midterm elections. He urged Republican voters to turn out, saying he could not "take a chance" on Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith losing her seat in the deep-red state.

The stop highlighted the difficulties Republicans face in an election that could drastically shift power in Washington. Republican candidates have struggled with online fundraising, leaving them more dependent on large donors and super PACs. Republicans argue the president's presence energizes the base and that the party can hold its majorities.

Democrats, for their part, are pointing to favorable polling, including a new NPR poll showing an advantage heading into Election Day, and are forming a congressional task force to protect the election. Both parties are using the final stretch to mobilize their voters, with control of Congress at stake and consequences for the remainder of Trump's term.

stories.headline: Truce Begins in Russian-Occupied Ukrainian City of Oleshky
stories.summary:
A limited ceasefire has begun in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity. Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the truce is being respected. The White House said it was secured by First Lady Melania Trump.

The truce is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation planned for Friday, as well as clearing of mines from roads. Ukraine estimates about 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in the city and surrounding areas, out of a prewar population of 24,000. Residents told the BBC they have cooked garden weeds to survive and want to leave.

Many fear the truce will not hold, and details of the evacuation remain unclear. Some worry Russia may bar returns or inspect phones for signs of Ukrainian support, while others fear shooting could resume and Kyiv be blamed. The Kremlin has acknowledged supply problems while blaming Kyiv. Verifying conditions is difficult because communications are patchy.

stories.headline: Update: Teen Charged as Adult in Florida A&M Homecoming Shooting That Wounded 11
stories.summary:
Police in Tallahassee say a 15-year-old has been charged as an adult in the weekend shooting that wounded 11 people at Florida A&M University after the school's homecoming football game. The teenager faces 11 counts of attempted second-degree murder and a count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent.

The charges follow the arrest of the suspect earlier this week. The shooting near the stadium during homecoming week injured a number of people, including children, and raised concerns about safety at campus events.

The case now moves through the adult court system. Authorities have not detailed a motive in the material available.
